title: Feynman diagrams and external potentials (Sec. 12.1 only)
scope: Sec. 12.1 (Eqs. 12.1-12.10): non-interacting fermions in an external potential. Secs. 12.2-12.6 are out of scope.

keyResults.name: Hamiltonian with external potential
keyResults.latex: $$H=H_0+V,\qquad V=\sum_\sigma\int d\mathbf r\,\Psi^\dagger_\sigma(\mathbf r)V_\sigma(\mathbf r)\Psi_\sigma(\mathbf r)$$

keyResults.name: Equation of motion for the full function
keyResults.note: Eq. (12.3b); same sign convention as Eq. (11.66).

keyResults.note: Eq. (12.6); each term is a sum over scattering events by V.

keyResults.note: Eqs. (12.7)-(12.8); internal vertices are integrated over 1.

keyResults.note: Eqs. (12.9)-(12.10); the integral form (12.5) is recovered from the diagrams.

questions.prompt: Write the integral Dyson equation for $\mathcal G(b,a)$ of non-interacting fermions in an external potential $V(1)$, and write its first two iterations in terms of $\mathcal G_0$.
questions.solution:
$$\mathcal G(b,a)=\mathcal G_0(b,a)+\int d1\,\mathcal G_0(b,1)V(1)\mathcal G(1,a)\qquad\text{(Eq. 12.5)}.$$
Inserting the equation into itself gives
$$\mathcal G(b,a)=\mathcal G_0(b,a)+\int d1\,\mathcal G_0(b,1)V(1)\mathcal G_0(1,a)+\int d1\,d2\,\mathcal G_0(b,1)V(1)\mathcal G_0(1,2)V(2)\mathcal G_0(2,a)+\cdots\quad\text{(Eq. 12.6)}.$$

questions.prompt: In the diagrams of Sec. 12.1 the external potential is drawn as a cross. What does an internal vertex with a cross mean?
choices: A fixed external point with no integration
An integral $\int d1$ over space and imaginary time with the factor $V(1)$ at that vertex
A sum over spin only, with no factor
A factor $-1$ for each closed fermion loop
questions.solution: Each internal vertex is integrated over $1=(\mathbf r_1,\sigma_1,\tau_1)$ and carries the factor $V(1)$ (Eqs. 12.7-12.8). The external points $a$ and $b$ are fixed. The other options describe other rules of the book.

questions.prompt: Book Exercise 12.1. One-dimensional electrons with $U(x)=U_0\delta(x)$ and $\hbar=1$. Use $v=k/m$ and the free retarded function $G^R_0(x,x',\omega)=-\frac{i}{v}e^{ik|x-x'|}$. Solve the Dyson equation for $x'<0<x$ and find the transmission amplitude $t$ and $|t|^2$.
questions.solution:
1. Dyson's equation with the delta potential gives $G(x,x')=G_0(x,x')+G_0(x,0)\,U_0\,G(0,x')$. Setting $x=0$ gives $G(0,x')=G_0(0,x')/[1-U_0G_0(0,0)]$.
2. With $G_0(0,0)=-i/v$, the denominator is $1+iU_0/v$.
3. For $x'<0<x$, $G_0(x,0)U_0G_0(0,x')=-(U_0/v^2)e^{ik(x-x')}$. Collecting terms, $G(x,x')=-\frac{i}{v}\,t\,e^{ik(x-x')}$ with
$$t=\frac{1}{1+iU_0/v},\qquad |t|^2=\frac{1}{1+(U_0/v)^2}.$$
This matches the barrier result of Ex. 7.2.

questions.prompt: Book Exercise 12.2 (resonant tunneling). The potential is $U_0[\delta(x-a_1)+\delta(x-a_2)]$. Define $\alpha=U_0/(iv)$ and $\theta=k(a_2-a_1)$, and use $G^R_0$ as in Ex. 12.1. For $x'<a_1<a_2<x$, show that $G^R=-\frac{i}{v}\,t\,e^{ik(x-x')}$ with $t=[(1-\alpha)^2-\alpha^2e^{2i\theta}]^{-1}$, and show that $|t|=1$ when $\alpha=i\cot\theta$.
questions.solution:
1. Write $G(x,x')=G_0(x,x')+\sum_j G_0(x,a_j)U_jG(a_j,x')$ with $G_0(x,x')=-\frac iv e^{ik|x-x'|}$. Put $\Phi_j=G(a_j,x')$, $E=e^{i\theta}$ and $\alpha_j=U_j/(iv)=U_jG_0(0,0)$. Setting $x=a_1,a_2$ gives the 2x2 system
$$(1-\alpha_1)\Phi_1-\alpha_2E\,\Phi_2=s_1,\qquad -\alpha_1E\,\Phi_1+(1-\alpha_2)\Phi_2=s_1E,\qquad s_1=-\tfrac iv e^{ik(a_1-x')}.$$
Its determinant is $D=(1-\alpha_1)(1-\alpha_2)-\alpha_1\alpha_2E^2$. Inserting $\Phi_{1,2}$ in $G(x,x')$ for $x>a_2$, the numerator collapses to 1, so
$$G^R(x,x')=-\frac iv\,t\,e^{ik(x-x')},\qquad t=\frac1D.$$
2. For equal barriers, $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha$, this is the stated $t=[(1-\alpha)^2-\alpha^2e^{2i\theta}]^{-1}$. For $U_2=0$ it reduces to $1/(1-\alpha_1)$, the single-barrier result of Ex. 12.1.
3. Put $\alpha=i\cot\theta$ into $D=(1-\alpha)^2-\alpha^2e^{2i\theta}$. Using $\alpha^2=-\cot^2\theta$ and $e^{2i\theta}-1=2i\sin\theta\,e^{i\theta}$ one finds $D=1-2\cos\theta\,e^{i\theta}$. Then $D=1-2\cos^2\theta-2i\sin\theta\cos\theta=-\cos2\theta-i\sin2\theta=-e^{2i\theta}$, so
$$|t|=1/|D|=1.$$
This is the resonance condition of the exercise (Eq. E.12.6). Physically, the two paths $x'\to a_1\to x$ and $x'\to a_1\to a_2\to a_1\to a_2\to x$ and all longer ones interfere constructively.
